power.title: Power Analysis Check
report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

text.text: Little is known about the dynamics of children's conversations outside of urban Western contexts, where research focuses on one-on-one interactions with parents.

Our study addresses this gap, aggregating naturalistic speech data gathered in 10 countries across multiple labs, and using novel speech diarization algorithms to extract and classify different types of conversation.
We analyzed 23,000 hours of child-centered audio recordings taken from 844 children (mean age 23 months; 389 girls) across urban, agricultural, and foraging societies.
We found that multiparty conversations, involving at least three speakers, are more frequent than any other type of conversation.
Across settings, children's relative exposure to conversation differed based on their age, number of siblings, and mother's education.
We conclude that the kinds of conversation most often studied differ from those children typically encounter.
Greater focus on children's conversations in multiparty contexts may provide a more representative picture of their daily experience with language.

Conversation is a cornerstone of human social interaction, with considerable evidence suggesting that human cognition is specifically geared toward back-and-forth linguistic exchanges (Levinson, 2016).

text.text: Home-based observational studies have found that more parent-child conversation is positively associated with children's language development (Hirsh-Pasek et al., 2015).

text.text: This is a potentially serious gap, as children's language is also impacted by who and how many people they are talking with.

For example, children have been found to produce more mental state vocabulary (i.e., referring to their own or somebody else's thoughts, as in I changed my mind) during conversations with friends and peers than with their mothers (Brown et al., 1996).

text.text: There are a number of possible explanations for these differences.
For instance, households in less urbanized societies tend to have more children.

Children with older siblings are also exposed to less child-directed speech from adults and more overheard speech directed to another child, compared to children without any siblings (Galindo & Montag, 2025).

text.text: These factors and their interactions might also account for varied patterns of conversation observed across different cultural settings.

Living in a society with fewer children per household may result in more exposure to speech from adults over time (as in Gilkerson et al., 2017), while living in a society with more siblings per home may result in less speech from adults but more with other children (as in Cristia et al., 2023).

text.text: Some recent studies have attempted to address these shortcomings by leveraging long-form audio corpora composed of daylong recordings from global samples of children.

In a large-scale study of child-centered adult speech in 12 countries, Bergelson et al. (2023) found that neither child age, gender, nor household education consistently predicted differences in speech input.

text.text: In another study, Bunce et al. (2024) compared child-directed and adult-directed speech in randomly sampled clips across five countries.

They found that children were exposed to more total speech during periods when more speakers were present, and that overall adult-directed speech, but not child-directed speech, increased with child age.
However, they did find that child-directed speech from other children increased relative to female adult speech with age.

By analyzing long-form audio data with a novel system for automatically classifying conversation, we gain a unique glimpse into children's daily verbal experiences, beyond their dyadic interactions with caregivers.
In this paper, we examine a massive cross-national dataset assembled as a part of a data-sharing initiative between a global consortium of researchers (EL1000 Consortium, 2026).

The diversity of home environments and caregiving practices represented by this dataset captures not only dyadic adult-child conversations, but also other, less explored types of interactions: child-child, multiparty, and overheard conversations.
We utilize speaker diarization algorithms to automatically classify different types of conversation in everyday speech, allowing us to analyze far more (https://doi.org/10.12751/g-node.ky76mk).

text.text: A full description of each corpus included in our analysis can be found in Supplementary Materials (S1).
Each of these studies used child-worn recording devices to collect audio from naturalistic home-based interactions throughout the day.
Studies were included based on the availability of information about the target child's age, gender, number of siblings, and maternal education.
These variables were selected for their potential impact on conversations in the home, as well as being the most commonly collected variables across corpora.

We excluded from the analysis children who had been identified by individual data curators as having atypical development that might have greatly affected their data, such as children with ASD or who are hard of hearing (n = 11 children).
In many cases, this was based on caregiver-reported information and may not reflect a diagnosis received after completion of the study.
Recordings of target children with missing data were excluded from the analysis (n = 31).
To ensure recordings were of sufficient length to calculate hourly rates, recordings less than one hour in length were also excluded (n = 4).

The resulting data are composed of 23087 hours of audio collected from 1820 recordings of children in households across 10 countries, spanning urban market-based societies and rural subsistence societies (Table 1).

Households varied greatly in size, with children reported as having anywhere between 0 to 8 siblings (mean = 1, SD = 2).
Educational attainment ranged from no formal schooling to professional degrees (mean = NA years, SD = 5) (Table 2; see Figure 2 for visualization).

text.text: The exact data collection procedure for each study is summarized in Supplementary Materials (S1).
In general, researchers placed a small audio recording device in or on the target child's shirt.

Depending on the study, the device was either a LENA© audio recording device (Gilkerson et al., 2017), an Olympus WS-832 (Olympus WS-832, Olympus Corporation, Tokyo, Japan), or a USB audio recording device (Cristia et al., 2023).

text.text: The device was typically active until the maximum recording duration (e.g., 15 hours in the case of the USBs) was reached or the device ran out of batteries or was picked up again by researchers, but in some cases, the researchers set a different target recording duration (e.g., 10 hrs total between 8am and 7pm for the Warlaumont corpus).
During this time, the device recorded ambient audio in the child's vicinity from the target child's perspective.
In some cases, caregivers were able to pause the recorder or request that sections be deleted due to privacy concerns.

Each audio recording was analyzed offline using Voice Type Classifier, an open-source speaker diarization software, to identify and diarize speech by different speaker categories (VTC2; Charlot et al., 2025).

text.text: VTC2 utilizes a machine learning approach called BabyHuBERT to derive speech representations thanks to pre-training on speech extracted from long-form recordings.

VTC2 was fine-tuned on human-annotated speech data from numerous languages (including languages as diverse as Taiwanese, Ju|'hoan, and Tsimane') representing at least six language families (Indo-European, Sino-Tibetan, Khoisan, Japonic, Mosetenan, and Austronesian).

VTC2 does not identify individual speakers; rather, it attempts to categorize vocalizations into one of four speaker classes: target child (i.e., the child wearing the recording device), female adults, male adults, and other children.

Unlike LENA, which treats all cases of overlap between any two classes as a single 'overlap' category, VTC2 allows speaker labels to overlap, providing start and end times for each individual voice type, which means that this overlap does not inflate non-speech estimates.
VTC2 has been shown to be more accurate than LENA in diarizing speech across all speaker categories, based on data from urban, English-speaking settings (Charlot et al., 2025).

text.text: Conversation metrics.
Conversational turns in each recording were quantified using the ChildProject package in Python (Gautheron et al., 2022).
text.formatted: Conversational turns in each recording were quantified using the ChildProject package in Python <ref type="bibr">(Gautheron et al., 2022)</ref>.

text.text: We define four classes of conversation, guided by the previous literature: adult-child (involving the target child and female or male adult(s)), child-child (target child and other child or children), multiparty (target child with an adult and another child, with two adults of different genders, or all speaker categories), and overheard (any conversation without target child).
As VTC2 can only distinguish between speaker categories, and not individual speakers, it was not possible to determine definitively how many speakers are present in a conversation.
For example, an adult-child conversation between the target child and a female adult could have more than one female adult speaker.
We return to this limitation and its impact on the interpretation of our results in the Discussion.

We also report the results of a follow-up analysis dividing multiparty conversations into adult-only interactions (i.e., target child, female adult, and male adult) and mixed age interactions (i.e., target child, other children, and adult(s)) in Supplementary Materials (S5).
To evaluate the validity of the conversation schema, we asked human annotators to manually classify 297 minutes of conversation in a series of audio clips taken from the Natovich corpus.
This corpus contained recordings of two-parent homes with two children, ensuring each possible type of conversation could be represented.

We used these annotations to gauge the accuracy of the automatic classifier while varying two parameters: how close in time vocalizations needed to occur to be considered a conversational turn (either 1s or 5s), and how much a speaker needed to contribute to a conversation to be considered a participant for the purposes of classification (between 1% and 20%).
We selected the values that maximized the average accuracy across all categories.

This resulted in a definition of conversation as any sequence of vocalizations by different participants that occur within 5 seconds of one another and a definition of participant as any speaker category that contributed to at least 6% of the total length of a conversation (Supplementary Materials S3).
Predictors.
We compared children's exposure to different forms of conversation to two child-level predictors: child age and sex; and two household-level predictors: number of siblings and maternal education.
Prior to formal analysis, we outlined several possible relationships between these factors and children's conversation which we detail in Supplementary Materials (S2).
Age was calculated across corpora by comparing the child's date of birth to the date of the recording session.

Because some studies reported years of education and others the highest attained education, we developed a schema to convert education to the desired format (e.g., high school degree = 12 years; bachelor's degree = 16 years), which we describe in Supplementary Materials (S3).

Educational norms differed greatly across studies: for example, not finishing secondary schooling would be considered a low amount of education in the US-based studies, whereas in other studies having any amount of secondary schooling would be considered highly educated.
As a result, we computed mothers' relative education within a study sample.

This was done by converting years of reported education to a z-score centered at zero, such that each point represented a standard deviation higher or lower educational attainment within that participant's study.

Although our samples did not necessarily represent the full range of education within each society, this approach allowed us to determine whether relative educational attainment related to conversational turns in the same way across corpora.

To determine whether highest attained education also predicted children's conversation, we conducted another analysis where education was treated as a categorical variable with three levels: less than secondary education, completed secondary education, and post-secondary education.
Because both analyses produced the same results, we report the results of this analysis in Supplementary Materials (S3).
The remaining variables were reported by researchers from the individual corpora.
We constructed mixed effects Bayesian regression models using the brms package, with conversational turn counts as the dependent variable (Bürkner, 2017).
text.formatted: We constructed mixed effects Bayesian regression models using the brms package, with conversational turn counts as the dependent variable <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">(Bürkner, 2017)</ref>.

text.text: We assumed a negative binomial distribution, which is used to model over-dispersed count data, where the variance is much greater than the mean.
This approach has been used in previous studies of language input derived from long-form audio recordings (e.g., Bunce et al., 2024).

text.text: To account for differences in conversational turn counts due to the length of individual audio recordings, we include an offset term for the log recording duration.

We fit a random intercept for corpus, to capture the variance different settings and study designs might have introduced, and, where applicable, a random intercept for child, to capture variance from multiple observations per child within corpora.
To capture variance in the relationships between conversation and our predictors across settings, we also fit our models with random slopes (Barr et al., 2013).

We first compared the frequency of different classes of conversation across societies by constructing a single model with conversation class (e.g. adult-child) as a predictor variable.
We selected adult-child conversation as the base comparison case, as it is the most commonly tracked form of conversation in child language studies.
Next, we re-examined our predictors across-corpora, constructing a single regression model for each conversation type that included data from all corpora.
This analysis was meant to find predictors of conversation that are consistent across societies.

In addition, we examined possible predictors of conversation within-corpus, constructing a separate set of models (one for each conversation class) containing each our four predictor variables (child age, sex, number of siblings, and maternal education).
This analysis allowed us to examine whether the presence of associations between conversation and the predictor variables differed across societies.
We report these results in Supplementary Materials (S6).
Each model was constructed by running four Markov chains for 4000 iterations each.
Model fit was assessed by performing posterior predictive checks.
Chain convergence was determined by ensuring all R = 1.
Given the large size of our dataset and the novelty of our analysis, we used weakly informative priors recommended by the brms package for negative binomial regression modeling.
Flat priors were used for predictor variables.

We report raw standardized coefficients (i.e., log increases in turns per hour) in our tables, and exponentiated coefficients (i.e., percentage increases in turns per hour) in the text for practical interpretation.
We also report the posterior mean and the highest density interval (HDI) at 95% for each coefficient.
To determine whether the evidence for an effect was compelling, we computed the posterior probability that the coefficient was greater than or less than 0.
Probabilities greater than 95% were considered strong evidence for an effect.

text.text: Child-level factors.
We found strong evidence that child age was associated with turns across different kinds of conversation.

Target older children were more likely to engage in child-child conversations (ß = 0.59, 95% HDI = [0.41, 0.79], pd > 0.999) and less likely to be exposed to overheard conversation (ß = -0.35, 95% HDI = [-0.52, -0.19], pd = 0).

text.text: Converting the log coefficients to probabilities by taking the exponent, we find that each SD increase in age within the sample predicts a 80% increase for child-child turns, and a 29% decrease in overheard turns.
No evidence for an association of conversational turns with child gender was found, suggesting no systematic differences in conversation for boys versus girls.
Household-level factors.
We found strong evidence that the number of siblings a child had was associated with conversational turns.

Children with more siblings were more likely to be exposed to multiparty conversations (ß = 0.09, 95% HDI = [-0.02, 0.21], pd = 0.956), child conversations (ß = 0.44, 95% HDI = [0, 0.88], pd = 0.975), and overheard conversation (ß = 0.09, 95% HDI = [0.02, 0.18], pd = 0.992), and were less likely to engage in adult-child conversation (ß = -0.21, 95% HDI = [-0.34, -0.11], pd = 0.001).

Each SD increase in sibship size resulted in a 10% increase in multiparty conversational turns, a 55% increase in child-child turns, a 10% increase in overheard turns, and a 19% decrease for adult-child turns.
Children whose mothers had relatively higher education engaged in less child-child conversation (ß = -0.17, 95% HDI = [-0.39, 0], pd = 0.974) (Table 4).
text.formatted: Children whose mothers had relatively higher education engaged in less child-child conversation (ß = -0.17, 95% HDI = [-0.39, 0], pd = 0.974) (Table <ref type="table">4</ref>).

text.text: This was equivalent to a 16% decrease in conversational turns.
No evidence for an association with other forms of conversation was found.
Children's engagement in child-child conversation was strongly related to almost every predictor.
We conducted follow-up analyses of statistical interactions that we hypothesized could be present based on prior research.
First, we modeled the interaction between child age and number of siblings.
We hypothesized that the positive relationship between child age and child-child conversation would be moderated by the presence of other children in the home.

After adding this term to our model, we found an over-additive interaction between the predictors, such that older children were exposed to even more child-child speech if they had more siblings (ß = -0.17, 95% HDI = [-0.38, 0], pd = 0.974).

However, we found little evidence that the interaction term improved the overall predictive accuracy of the model, as measured via Bayesian leave-one-out (LOO) cross validation (ELPD difference = -1.23, SE difference = 3.26).
Next, we modeled the interaction between maternal education and number of siblings.

We hypothesized that the negative relationship between maternal education and child-child conversation could be moderated by the negative relationship between maternal education and number of siblings.

We found that having more siblings reduced the negative relationship between education and child-child conversation (ß = 0.14, 95% HDI = [0.03, 0.29], pd = 0.966), indicating that the influence of education on child conversation is strongly tied to its relationship to family size.
As with our previous analysis, adding this term to the model did not noticeably improve model fit (ELPD difference = 0.14, SE difference = 2.92).
Thus, while we found more complex interactions between our predictor variables, we did not find that they substantially improved the fit of our predictive models.
In our analysis of 844 children from 13 studies, spanning 10 countries, we explored how children's experiences with different forms of conversation varied within and across settings.
We found that across these societies as a whole, children much more often engaged in multiparty conversations than they did in dyadic conversations.

This is a striking finding given the overwhelming prevalence of research on one-on-one interactions between a mother and a child (Coffey & Snedeker, 2026), and the relatively scarce research on interactions with multiple speakers.

text.text: Multiparty interactions are potentially a rich source of linguistic input to children, having been found to elicit more speech from young children and exposing them to a wider range of words (Barton & Tomasello, 1991; Rabain-Jamin, 2001; Oshima-Takane & Robbins, 2003).

text.text: It is also notable that the frequency of multiparty conversations was not specific to rural, non-Western samples, which are more associated with these types of interactions (e.g., Schieffelin & Ochs, 1986).

text.text: Rather, even in our U.S. and Canadian samples, multiparty conversation was as common or more than adult-child conversation.
The consistency of this pattern suggests that multiparty interactions may be equally impactful across cultural settings.

Indeed, children's language skills have been directly linked to their exposure to child-directed speech in multiparty situations (Ramírez-Esparza et al., 2017), and in households with multiple adults, children's vocabulary is better predicted by total input than by input from the primary caregiver alone (Shneidman et al., 2013).

text.text: Overheard and child-child conversation varied greatly in frequency across corpora.
The influence of these forms of speech on children's language development has been widely debated.

While there is not much evidence that either of these forms of speech predict individual differences in children's performance on tests of language ability (Coffey & Snedeker, 2026), children have been shown to learn words from overheard speech in both lab-based studies (e.g., Floor & Akhtar, 2006) and naturalistic contexts (Foushee & Srinivasan, 2024).

text.text: Likewise, children have been found to attend closely to speech produced by other children (Schick et al., 2025), and in some instances learn preferentially from child speech over adult speech (Erskine & Seidl, 2026).

text.text: In addition, both overheard and child speech have been found to predict differences in children's vocal activity (Schick & Stoll, 2025; Coffey et al., 2026).
text.formatted: In addition, both overheard and child speech have been found to predict differences in children's vocal activity <ref type="bibr" target="#b49">(Schick & Stoll, 2025;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">Coffey et al., 2026)</ref>.

text.text: Both forms of interaction are also related to multiparty conversation; many multiparty interactions may originate as overheard interaction that children interject in or are invited to join.

Multiparty interactions may also serve as vehicles for children to engage more closely with both adults and other children simultaneously which may have implications for various other aspects of child development.

Taken together, our results suggest a gap between the contexts in which language acquisition is most frequently studied (dyadic interactions with adults) and those in which children most frequently encounter speech (multiparty interactions with adults and peers).
In the analysis of child-level predictors, older children were found to engage in more child-child conversation than younger children.

Some previous studies have found that children spend more time with other children as they grow older, particularly in smaller-scale rural societies, resulting in more child-directed speech from these sources (Shneidman & Goldin-Meadow, 2012; Cristia et al., 2019; Loukatou et al., 2022).

text.text: Our findings suggest that this trend also persists when factoring in larger-scale industrialized societies.
Older children also encountered less overheard conversation as they grew older.
This may be because children's growing language skills allow for greater participation in nearby conversations.

There was no evidence for age associations with adult-child conversation, aligning with the results of a recent global study that found no consistent association between child age and adult vocalizations across countries (Bergelson et al., 2023; Bunce et al., 2024).

text.text: No effect of child gender was found, suggesting that boys and girls experience similar amounts of conversation across the societies surveyed (similar to Bergelson et al., 2023).

text.text: Future research could examine how children's participation in conversation was impacted by differences in their developmental status.
A previous study found that children's vocal activity, but not their adult speech input, was negatively associated with atypical development (Bergelson et al., 2023).
text.formatted: A previous study found that children's vocal activity, but not their adult speech input, was negatively associated with atypical development <ref type="bibr">(Bergelson et al., 2023)</ref>.

text.text: As a result, we might expect that children at risk of language delay may engage in less conversation in total, but potentially be exposed to more overheard conversation.

In the analysis of household-level predictors, children with more siblings were found to experience more total turns in all types of conversation, except for adult-child conversation, which they experienced less of.
Intuitively, children with more siblings would have more opportunities to engage in conversation with other children.

There would also be fewer opportunities to engage in one-on-one conversations with adults, but more opportunities for joint multiparty conversations and to observe conversations between adults and other children.

Our findings suggest that the presence of children may have a complex association with children's early language environments, changing not only how often children are able to converse with each other, but also the ways in which they typically engage with their adult caregivers.
These patterns may also change with the age of other children in their homes.
Children with older siblings might find themselves being watched more often by other children than by adults, and children with younger siblings may find themselves acting as babysitters.

In either case we would expect more child-child conversation, but in the former scenario the target child would receive more speech input from other children, while in the latter they would serve as sources of speech input for their younger charges.

Thus, researchers examining the influence of siblings on children's language exposure should note the age of other children living in the home and if possible whether they have responsibilities that would make them less present in the key child's environment, such as schooling.
Children whose mothers had higher education, both relative to their populations and overall, engaged in less child-child conversation.

Although previous studies have found that more highly educated mothers tend to have fewer children, this effect persisted for both definitions of education even after controlling for children's number of siblings.

There was also strong evidence of an interaction (albeit one that did not improve model predictiveness), suggesting that education was relatively less related to lower child-child conversation in homes with more siblings.

One possible interpretation of these findings is that education changes parent behavior in the presence of other children, such that more educated mothers might converse with their children more often.
Depending on the household, this could result in more adult-child, multiparty, or overheard conversation, but would uniformly reduce the amount of child-child conversations across homes.
There was also no evidence that education was related to adult-child conversation.

Previous studies have found both positive associations (Piot et al., 2022) and negative associations between speech input and education (Ma et al., 2024), and it is likely that the relationship between these variables is contingent on the broader socioeconomic context of the communities to which families belong (e.g., active vs. passive urbanization, see Ju et al., 2025).

text.text: There are some important limitations to note in our analysis.

First, the classification of conversation is a difficult problem in speaker diarization, as traditional definitions of conversation rely on information that these algorithms do not have access to (e.g., what is being said, who is the addressee).
Even for conversational turns, which only rely on the temporal co-occurrence of speech, accuracy estimates are generally lower than those for raw vocalizations (Ferjan Ramírez et al., 2021).
text.formatted: Even for conversational turns, which only rely on the temporal co-occurrence of speech, accuracy estimates are generally lower than those for raw vocalizations <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">(Ferjan Ramírez et al., 2021)</ref>.

text.text: While we were able to approximate the accuracy of classification for different types of conversation, this estimation was limited to speech samples from one corpus with an unusually uniform household structure (i.e., each speaker category was present and each had only one representative).
We do not know the degree to which the thresholds we selected for conversational turn latency and participation vary cross-culturally.
As a result, the values that maximized accuracy in this corpus might not do so in other corpora.
Even if these values were consistent across corpora, any amount of classification inaccuracy could skew the results of the analysis.
In light of this, our findings should be interpreted judiciously, particularly for overheard conversation, which was found to have the lowest overall accuracy (Supplementary Materials S3).

Second, the multiparty speech category, as we have defined it, is fundamentally limited by the use of a voice type classifier, which can only segment audio by speaker category (e.g., female or male adult), as opposed to a speaker diarizer which segments audio by individual speakers (e.g., mother and grandmother).
As an example, what looks like a conversation between the target child and a female adult may actually involve multiple female adults that are not differentiated by the classifier.
In societies where children receive large amounts of care from several female adult relatives, this constraint would result in the underestimation of multiparty conversation.

Third and relatedly, the multiparty category contains many different possible speaker combinations: two children and an adult, male and female adult and the key child, as male adult with two children, female adult and two children, or all speaker categories.
These types of multiparty subcategories may differ in key aspects.

For instance, while there was strong evidence to suggest that children with more siblings engage in more multiparty conversation, the same was not true when examining a sub-category containing the target child and at least one male and one female adult (see Supplementary Materials S5).

text.text: Lastly, there may be differences in exposure to conversation across corpora that result from differences in how data was collected, rather than differences inherent to the daily lives of the families involved.
Although all families were asked to record children for as much of the day as possible in or around the home, there were differences in the contexts in which recordings took place.
Other differences in conversation might result from constraints on the kinds of data that can be collected across settings.
For instance, children from more urban settings might spend more of their time in daycare or preschool settings than children in more rural settings.
These settings are particularly rich in child-child conversation (Soderstrom & Wittebole, 2013; Perry et al., 2018).
text.formatted: These settings are particularly rich in child-child conversation <ref type="bibr">(Soderstrom & Wittebole, 2013;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b41">Perry et al., 2018)</ref>.

text.text: However, due to the difficulty of collecting data in these settings, which typically requires consent from both the institution and all families whose children may potentially be recorded, most studies request that families only record their children at home.

This may result in an underestimation of child-child conversation in urban communities relative to rural communities, where children more often spend time with other children outside of these settings.
Our adaptation of recently developed speech diarization software gives us a unique glimpse into the daily lives of children growing up around the world.
We developed a coding scheme that allowed us to capture more diverse forms of conversation than are typically captured in traditional studies of child speech.
We found that adult-child conversations were less common than multiparty conversation across almost all corpora.
We found evidence for consistent predictors of conversation across highly diverse child populations, with some findings running contrary to accepted wisdom in studies of childhood conversation.
Notably, we failed to find strong evidence that maternal education was positively related to adult-child conversation, using both relative and absolute measures of educational attainment.
We believe these findings speak to the strength of using long-form audio recording analysis to study child conversations in different settings.

We hope to inspire more collaborative and interdisciplinary efforts to establish more generalizable theories of language development through the construction and analysis of large cross-cultural datasets.
